outcomes: Compute confusion counts, precision, recall, and F1 from model scores without hiding threshold choices.
Compare class-weighted loss and weighted sampling while explaining how each changes the effective training distribution.

sections.title: Measure prevalence before choosing an intervention
sections.summary: A high accuracy can describe a model that predicts only the common negative class.
body: Count positive and negative candidates by split and by independent source identity. Then evaluate the Chapter 13 checkpoint with its unchanged decision rule. Record confusion counts as integers before deriving ratios, because they expose what an apparently good percentage represents.

Keep raw logits or positive-class scores alongside labels and identities. Those scores support threshold analysis later; storing only hard predictions destroys information and encourages retraining for what is actually a decision-policy question.

sections.title: Separate ranking quality from the operating threshold
sections.summary: A model emits scores; the threshold converts them into actions with different false-positive and false-negative costs.
body: Precision is TP/(TP+FP), recall is TP/(TP+FN), and F1 is their harmonic mean. Compute them across a validation threshold grid and visualize the tradeoff. Choose a rule using validation data only, such as maximum F1 or a minimum recall constraint, and write that rule before evaluating test labels.

Use a small epsilon only to define numerical behavior, not to conceal an empty prediction set. For a series-level objective, aggregate candidate scores according to the predefined project contract before computing the final metrics.

code.title: Compute stable binary metrics
code.source:
import torch

def precision_recall_f1(tp, fp, fn):
    tp = torch.as_tensor(tp, dtype=torch.float64)
    fp = torch.as_tensor(fp, dtype=torch.float64, device=tp.device)
    fn = torch.as_tensor(fn, dtype=torch.float64, device=tp.device)

    predicted_positive = tp + fp
    actual_positive = tp + fn
    precision = torch.where(
        predicted_positive > 0,
        tp / predicted_positive.clamp_min(1),
        torch.zeros_like(tp),
    )
    recall = torch.where(
        actual_positive > 0,
        tp / actual_positive.clamp_min(1),
        torch.zeros_like(tp),
    )
    pr_sum = precision + recall
    f1 = torch.where(
        pr_sum > 0,
        2 * precision * recall / pr_sum.clamp_min(torch.finfo(pr_sum.dtype).eps),
        torch.zeros_like(pr_sum),
    )
    return precision, recall, f1

sections.title: Understand what class weighting changes
sections.summary: A class-weighted loss changes the penalty attached to examples while leaving the loader distribution unchanged.
body: CrossEntropyLoss accepts one weight per class. Increasing the positive weight increases the contribution of positive errors to the batch loss and its gradients. Calculate weights from the training partition only, log them with the run, and compare against an unweighted baseline from the same initialization.

Weighting is not a metric and does not guarantee calibrated probabilities. It changes the optimization objective, so choose the deployment threshold again on validation scores rather than assuming 0.5 remains optimal.

sections.title: Use sampling as a separate experimental lever
sections.summary: WeightedRandomSampler changes which examples appear and how often, rather than changing their loss coefficient after loading.
body: Assign a sampling weight to each training example, normally inverse to its class frequency, and draw a controlled number of samples with replacement. Record the resulting class mix per epoch and remember that the same rare example may be visited repeatedly.

Do not combine weighted sampling and weighted loss by habit. Their effects multiply and may overcorrect. Compare baseline, loss weighting, sampling, and their combination as four explicit treatments under the same split and evaluation rule.

sections.title: Augment anatomy without changing the label contract
sections.summary: Random transformations are useful only when their geometry, interpolation, and intensity behavior remain plausible.
body: Apply small translations, rotations, flips only where orientation permits, scaling, and controlled intensity noise to training samples. For 3D CT crops, use tested tensor operations that transform all related targets consistently. Do not apply a 2D image transform to each slice independently when that breaks 3D structure.

TorchVision transforms v2 are the recommended current API for ordinary images and paired masks, and Chapter 15 uses that capability for 2D segmentation. The book's 3D CT path still needs domain-specific transforms with explicit interpolation and padding. Save grids of repeated transformations for positive and negative candidates.
points: Never augment validation or test samples stochastically.
Use nearest-neighbor interpolation for discrete masks.
Transform image and target geometry with the same random parameters.
Seed the augmentation path for regression tests.

callouts.title: A plausible image can carry a wrong label
callouts.body: Visual quality alone is insufficient. Verify that the candidate remains in the crop and that orientation-dependent transformations are permitted by the task.

sections.title: Turn improvements into controlled comparisons
sections.summary: One-factor ablations and frozen evaluation rules are more informative than an untraceable pile of tricks.
body: Begin every treatment from the same base checkpoint or recorded initialization, data split, number of optimizer updates, and validation protocol. Change one primary factor, repeat across more than one seed where practical, and report both the primary metric and confusion counts.

Choose the checkpoint and threshold on validation data. Evaluate the held-out test partition once for the final comparison, then report false-positive and false-negative examples with source identities. If the test result prompts a design change, that creates a new experiment and requires a new untouched test set or transparent exploratory status.
